Engineering Student Guidance Assistant - Knowledge Base - Page 1
Engineering Student Guidance Assistant
Knowledge Base and Teaching Document for the RAG Application
This document is the knowledge source for an AI assistant that helps new students choose an engineering
field. The assistant first collects a short student introduction, then asks which engineering domain the
student wants, and then teaches that domain step by step with lessons, examples and practice questions.
All answers must follow the rules in Part 1.
Part 1: Rules and Code of Conduct
The assistant and every student using it must follow these rules at all times.
 Rule 1 - No bad words. Abusive, insulting, vulgar or offensive language is not allowed. If a student
uses bad words, the assistant politely warns the student once and asks them to continue respectfully.
After repeated misuse, the assistant stops giving guidance until respectful language is used.
 Rule 2 - Respect. Be respectful to the assistant, teachers, staff and other students. Bullying, ragging,
discrimination and hate speech are strictly prohibited.
 Rule 3 - Honesty. Students must give true and correct information in their introduction. False
information can lead to cancellation of the application.
 Rule 4 - Privacy. The assistant asks only for details required for guidance. Students should not share
passwords, bank details or OTPs. Personal data is used only for admission guidance.
 Rule 5 - Stay on topic. The assistant answers questions about admission, engineering fields,
eligibility, subjects, skills and careers, and teaches lessons in the student's chosen domain. Unrelated
or harmful requests are politely declined.
 Rule 6 - Academic integrity. Cheating, copying and plagiarism are not allowed during studies or
exams.
 Rule 7 - No guarantees. The assistant gives guidance, not guarantees of seats, marks, placements or
salary. Final admission and branch allotment decisions belong to the institute.
 Rule 8 - Proper use. Do not misuse the assistant, the internet, computers or lab equipment in any way.
 Rule 9 - Unknown answers. If the answer is not in this document, the assistant says it does not have
that information and suggests contacting the admission office. It must not invent facts.
Part 2: Student Introduction (First Step)
Before recommending any engineering field, the assistant must first ask the student for an introduction.
The assistant asks politely, one or two questions at a time, in this order.
Required details
 Full name - as on official ID or certificates.
 Age and date of birth.
 Gender (optional to answer).
 Contact details - mobile number and email address.
 City, state and country of residence.
 Parent or guardian name and contact number.
 Last qualification - for example 12th standard or Diploma, with board or university name.
 School or college name and year of passing.
 Marks, percentage or CGPA, including marks in Physics, Chemistry and Mathematics.
 Entrance exam and score or rank, if any (for example JEE or a state CET).

Engineering Student Guidance Assistant - Knowledge Base - Page 2
Interest questions asked after the introduction
 Which subjects do you enjoy most: Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry, Biology or Computer Science?
 Do you prefer coding and software, building machines, electronics and circuits, construction, or working
in labs?
 What is your career goal: job in industry, higher studies, research, government service or starting your
own business?
 Which engineering field do you already have in mind, if any?
Sample welcome message
"Welcome! I am your Engineering Guidance Assistant. Please keep the conversation respectful and free of
bad words. To begin, may I know your full name and age?"
Part 3: Conversation Flow - Ask, Guide, then Teach
The assistant follows these steps in order. It asks one or two questions at a time and waits for the answer.
 Step 1 - Greet and state the rules. Remind the student to avoid bad words and to be honest.
 Step 2 - Collect the introduction described in Part 2.
 Step 3 - Ask the domain. Ask: "Which engineering domain would you like to learn about?" and show
the list of domains from Part 4. If the student is not sure, ask the interest questions and suggest one to
three domains with reasons.
 Step 4 - Ask the level. Ask whether the student is a beginner, intermediate or advanced in that
domain.
 Step 5 - Show the roadmap. Retrieve the Teaching Module of the chosen domain from Part 5 and
share the learning roadmap for the student's level.
 Step 6 - Teach one concept at a time. Explain the concept in simple words suited to the student's age
and qualification, give a real-life example, then ask one small check question and wait for the answer.
 Step 7 - Give feedback. If the answer is right, praise and move on. If wrong, explain again in a different
way with another example. Never mock the student.
 Step 8 - Practice. After 3 to 4 concepts, ask the practice questions of the module and suggest the mini
project.
 Step 9 - Summarise and continue. Give a short summary of what was learned. Ask whether the
student wants the next level, another domain, or admission guidance for this branch.
Teaching style rules
 Use simple language first, then technical terms. Use the student's name to keep the lesson friendly.
 Teach only one concept per message. Keep messages short and use small examples or numbers.
 Answer using the Teaching Module and Part 4. If the student asks something deeper than the notes,
say clearly that it goes beyond the available material, give the best basic explanation, and suggest
textbooks or the faculty.
 Encourage hands-on practice with the mini project. For cyber security, teach only legal and ethical
practice.
 If the student uses bad words or asks for harmful help, follow Rule 1 and Rule 5 in Part 1.
Sample teaching dialogue
Assistant: Thanks, Ravi! Which engineering domain would you like to learn about?
Student: Electronics and Communication.
Assistant: Great choice. Are you a beginner, intermediate or advanced in this domain?
Student: Beginner.

Engineering Student Guidance Assistant - Knowledge Base - Page 3
Assistant: Let us start with Ohm's law. It says V = I x R: voltage equals current times resistance. If a 10 V
battery is connected to a 5 ohm resistor, what current flows?
Student: 2 amperes.
Assistant: Correct, well done! Now the next concept: the diode.
Eligibility rules common to all branches
 Standard eligibility for a B.E. / B.Tech degree is a pass in 12th standard with Physics and Mathematics,
plus Chemistry, Biology, Computer Science or a technical subject, with the minimum marks set by the
institute.
 Diploma holders may be eligible for lateral entry into the second year, as per institute and university
rules.
 Courses normally take 4 years (8 semesters); lateral entry takes 3 years.
 Minimum marks, seat numbers and cut-offs differ by institute and year, so the assistant advises the
student to confirm them with the admission office.

Engineering Student Guidance Assistant - Knowledge Base - Page 4
Part 4: Engineering Fields
Each field below is a separate section with the same structure: overview, subjects, skills, careers, higher
studies and who should choose it.
Field: Computer Science and Engineering (CSE)
Overview: Computer Science and Engineering deals with software, programming, algorithms, data and
computer systems. It is the base for apps, websites, games, cloud services and artificial intelligence.
Core subjects: Programming (C, Python, Java), data structures, algorithms, operating systems,
databases, computer networks, software engineering, theory of computation.
Skills needed: Logical thinking, problem solving, coding, mathematics, patience for debugging.
Career options: Software developer, web or mobile app developer, cloud engineer, database
administrator, DevOps engineer, game developer, product engineer.
Higher studies: M.Tech or MS in Computer Science, MBA, research in computing.
Best suited for: students who enjoy coding, logic puzzles, and building software or apps.
Field: Information Technology (IT)
Overview: Information Technology focuses on building, managing and securing information systems used
by businesses and organisations. It is very close to CSE but puts more weight on applications, networks
and system management.
Core subjects: Programming, web technologies, databases, networking, information security, cloud
computing, software testing, IT project management.
Skills needed: Programming, system administration, communication, teamwork, attention to detail.
Career options: Web developer, system administrator, network engineer, IT consultant, software tester,
business analyst.
Higher studies: M.Tech in IT, MBA in Information Systems, certifications in cloud and networking.
Best suited for: students who like technology in business and want strong job options in the IT industry.
Field: Artificial Intelligence and Data Science (AI and DS)
Overview: This field teaches how to make computers learn from data. It covers machine learning, deep
learning, data analysis and intelligent systems such as chatbots, recommendation systems and image
recognition.
Core subjects: Python, statistics, probability, linear algebra, machine learning, deep learning, data
mining, natural language processing, big data.
Skills needed: Strong mathematics, statistics, Python, curiosity, analytical thinking.
Career options: Data scientist, machine learning engineer, AI engineer, data analyst, NLP engineer,
computer vision engineer.
Higher studies: M.Tech or MS in AI, Data Science or Machine Learning, PhD research.
Best suited for: students who love mathematics, data and want to work on modern AI technology.

Engineering Student Guidance Assistant - Knowledge Base - Page 5
Field: Cyber Security
Overview: Cyber Security protects computers, networks and data from hackers and attacks. Students
learn how attacks work and how to defend systems legally and ethically.
Core subjects: Networking, cryptography, ethical hacking, operating system security, digital forensics,
malware analysis, security auditing.
Skills needed: Networking knowledge, curiosity, ethical mindset, careful and patient analysis.
Career options: Security analyst, ethical hacker or penetration tester, forensic investigator, security
consultant.
Higher studies: M.Tech in Cyber Security, security certifications, research in cryptography.
Best suited for: students who enjoy puzzles, networks and protecting systems, and who follow ethical
rules strictly.
Field: Electronics and Communication Engineering (ECE)
Overview: ECE covers electronic circuits, communication systems, signal processing and embedded
devices. It powers mobiles, satellites, Wi-Fi, televisions and the Internet of Things.
Core subjects: Analog and digital electronics, signals and systems, communication systems,
microprocessors, VLSI design, embedded systems, antennas, control systems.
Skills needed: Circuit design, mathematics, hardware debugging, embedded programming.
Career options: Electronics engineer, embedded systems engineer, VLSI designer, telecom engineer,
IoT engineer, satellite communication engineer.
Higher studies: M.Tech in VLSI, Communication or Embedded Systems, MS abroad, research.
Best suited for: students who like gadgets, circuits, mobile networks and hardware with some
programming.
Field: Electrical and Electronics Engineering (EEE)
Overview: EEE deals with generation, transmission and use of electrical power, electrical machines and
electronic controls. It is key for power plants, electric vehicles and renewable energy.
Core subjects: Circuit theory, electrical machines, power systems, power electronics, control systems,
measurements, renewable energy.
Skills needed: Mathematics, problem solving, safety awareness, understanding of machines and circuits.
Career options: Power engineer, electrical design engineer, electric vehicle engineer, automation
engineer, government power sector roles.
Higher studies: M.Tech in Power Systems or Power Electronics, MBA, competitive exams for public
sector jobs.
Best suited for: students interested in electricity, electric vehicles, power plants and renewable energy.

Engineering Student Guidance Assistant - Knowledge Base - Page 6
Field: Mechanical Engineering
Overview: Mechanical Engineering is about designing, building and maintaining machines, engines, tools
and manufacturing systems. It is one of the broadest branches.
Core subjects: Engineering mechanics, thermodynamics, fluid mechanics, machine design,
manufacturing processes, heat transfer, CAD and CAM, materials.
Skills needed: Design thinking, CAD software, mathematics, practical hands-on skills.
Career options: Design engineer, manufacturing engineer, maintenance engineer, automobile engineer,
HVAC engineer, production manager.
Higher studies: M.Tech in Thermal, Design or Manufacturing, MBA, MS abroad.
Best suited for: students who like machines, vehicles, tools and understanding how things work.
Field: Civil Engineering
Overview: Civil Engineering plans, designs and builds structures such as buildings, roads, bridges, dams,
water supply and drainage systems.
Core subjects: Structural analysis, surveying, concrete technology, geotechnical engineering,
transportation engineering, environmental engineering, estimation and costing.
Skills needed: Structural design, surveying, AutoCAD and design software, site management.
Career options: Site engineer, structural engineer, construction manager, urban planner, government
engineering services, consultant.
Higher studies: M.Tech in Structural or Transportation Engineering, MBA in construction management.
Best suited for: students interested in buildings, infrastructure, city planning and outdoor site work.
Field: Chemical Engineering
Overview: Chemical Engineering uses chemistry, physics and mathematics to turn raw materials into
useful products such as fuels, medicines, plastics, food and fertilisers on a large scale.
Core subjects: Chemical process calculations, fluid mechanics, heat and mass transfer, reaction
engineering, process control, process design.
Skills needed: Chemistry, mathematics, process thinking, safety discipline.
Career options: Process engineer, plant engineer, production engineer, quality engineer, research
engineer in petrochemical, pharma and food industries.
Higher studies: M.Tech in Chemical Engineering, MBA, research.
Best suited for: students who enjoy chemistry and want to work in industries and plants.
Field: Aerospace and Aeronautical Engineering
Overview: This field covers the design, building and testing of aircraft, rockets, satellites and drones.
Core subjects: Aerodynamics, aircraft structures, propulsion, flight mechanics, avionics, materials, control
systems.
Skills needed: Strong physics and mathematics, simulation software, precision and teamwork.
Career options: Aircraft design engineer, propulsion engineer, avionics engineer, drone engineer, roles in
space and defence organisations.
Higher studies: M.Tech or MS in Aerospace, PhD, research in space technology.
Best suited for: students fascinated by aeroplanes, rockets, space and drones.

Engineering Student Guidance Assistant - Knowledge Base - Page 7
Field: Automobile Engineering
Overview: Automobile Engineering deals with the design, manufacturing and servicing of cars, bikes and
trucks, including modern electric and hybrid vehicles.
Core subjects: Automotive engines, vehicle dynamics, transmission systems, automotive electronics,
electric vehicles, vehicle design.
Skills needed: Mechanical fundamentals, CAD, interest in vehicles, diagnostic skills.
Career options: Vehicle design engineer, R and D engineer, electric vehicle engineer, service and quality
engineer in the automobile industry.
Higher studies: M.Tech in Automotive Engineering, MBA, MS abroad.
Best suited for: students passionate about cars, bikes and electric vehicles.
Field: Mechatronics and Robotics Engineering
Overview: This field combines mechanical, electronics and computer engineering to build robots and
automated machines.
Core subjects: Sensors and actuators, robotics, control systems, embedded programming, PLC and
automation, machine design, machine vision.
Skills needed: Mixed skills in mechanics, electronics and coding, creativity, practical building ability.
Career options: Robotics engineer, automation engineer, PLC programmer, industrial automation
specialist, drone and robot developer.
Higher studies: M.Tech in Robotics or Automation, research in intelligent systems.
Best suited for: students who like building robots, automation and projects that mix hardware and
software.
Field: Biomedical Engineering
Overview: Biomedical Engineering applies engineering to medicine and healthcare. It develops medical
devices such as ECG machines, scanners, prosthetics and monitoring equipment.
Core subjects: Human anatomy and physiology, biomedical instrumentation, biomaterials, medical
imaging, biosignal processing, rehabilitation engineering.
Skills needed: Electronics, biology interest, accuracy, willingness to work with doctors.
Career options: Medical device engineer, clinical engineer, hospital equipment specialist, biomedical
researcher.
Higher studies: M.Tech in Biomedical Engineering, MS abroad, research.
Best suited for: students who want to combine engineering with healthcare.

Engineering Student Guidance Assistant - Knowledge Base - Page 8
Field: Biotechnology Engineering
Overview: Biotechnology Engineering uses living cells and biological processes to make medicines,
vaccines, food products and clean energy.
Core subjects: Cell biology, genetics, biochemistry, microbiology, bioprocess engineering, bioinformatics,
genetic engineering.
Skills needed: Biology and chemistry knowledge, lab skills, patience, research mindset.
Career options: Biotech researcher, bioprocess engineer, quality control analyst, bioinformatics specialist
in pharma and agriculture industries.
Higher studies: M.Tech or MSc in Biotechnology, PhD, research abroad.
Best suited for: students who love biology and lab-based research.
Field: Industrial and Production Engineering
Overview: This field improves how products are made and how factories and organisations work, with
focus on efficiency, quality, cost and supply chain.
Core subjects: Manufacturing processes, operations research, quality control, supply chain management,
work study, industrial automation.
Skills needed: Analytical thinking, management skills, planning, problem solving.
Career options: Production engineer, quality manager, supply chain analyst, operations manager,
industrial consultant.
Higher studies: M.Tech in Industrial Engineering, MBA in operations.
Best suited for: students who like planning, efficiency and both technical and management work.
Field: Environmental Engineering
Overview: Environmental Engineering works on clean water, waste management, pollution control and
sustainable development.
Core subjects: Water and wastewater treatment, air pollution control, solid waste management,
environmental impact assessment, sustainability.
Skills needed: Environmental awareness, chemistry and civil basics, field work, regulation knowledge.
Career options: Environmental engineer, water treatment engineer, sustainability consultant, pollution
control board officer.
Higher studies: M.Tech in Environmental Engineering, research, public sector roles.
Best suited for: students who care about nature, clean energy and sustainability.

Engineering Student Guidance Assistant - Knowledge Base - Page 9
Part 5: Domain Teaching Modules
After the student chooses a domain, the assistant uses the matching module below to teach. Each module
has a learning roadmap, concepts to teach one by one, a mini project and practice questions with
answers.
Teaching Module: Computer Science and Engineering
Learning roadmap
 Beginner: How computers work, Python basics, variables, loops, functions, basic problem solving.
 Intermediate: Data structures (list, stack, queue, tree), object-oriented programming, SQL databases,
Git.
 Advanced: Algorithms and complexity, operating systems, computer networks, web development,
system design.
Concepts to teach (in order)
1. Variable and data type: A variable is a named box that stores a value, such as a number, text or
true/false. Example: age = 18 stores the number 18.
2. Loop: A loop repeats instructions many times. Example: printing the numbers 1 to 10 with a for loop
instead of writing ten print lines.
3. Function: A function is a reusable block of code that takes input and gives output. Example: a
function that takes marks and returns the grade.
4. Stack and queue: A stack follows Last In First Out, like a pile of plates. A queue follows First In First
Out, like people standing in a line.
5. Algorithm and Big-O: An algorithm is a step-by-step method to solve a problem. Big-O describes
how the running time grows as input grows. Linear search is O(n); binary search on sorted data is O(log
n), which is much faster.
Mini project: Build a student marks calculator in Python, then a simple to-do list web app with a database.
Practice questions
 Q: What is the time complexity of binary search? Answer: O(log n). It needs the data to be sorted.
 Q: What is the difference between a stack and a queue? Answer: A stack is Last In First Out; a queue
is First In First Out.
 Q: What is SQL used for? Answer: To store, query and manage data in relational databases.
Teaching Module: Information Technology
Learning roadmap
 Beginner: Computer and internet basics, HTML and CSS, basic networking, using Linux commands.
 Intermediate: JavaScript, databases, web servers, cloud basics, software testing.
 Advanced: System administration, network security, DevOps, cloud architecture, IT project
management.
Concepts to teach (in order)
1. Client-server model: A client such as your browser sends a request, and a server sends back a
response. Websites work this way.
2. IP address and DNS: An IP address identifies a device on a network. DNS works like a phone book
that converts a website name into an IP address.
3. Database and SQL: A database stores organised data in tables. SQL is the language used to read
and change that data.

Engineering Student Guidance Assistant - Knowledge Base - Page 10
4. Cloud computing: Using servers and software over the internet instead of owning them. IaaS gives
infrastructure, PaaS gives a platform to build apps, SaaS gives ready software such as Gmail.
5. Software testing: Checking that software works correctly before release. Includes unit testing,
integration testing and user acceptance testing.
Mini project: Create a simple website with a login page connected to a database.
Practice questions
 Q: What does DNS do? Answer: It translates domain names into IP addresses.
 Q: Give an example of SaaS. Answer: Gmail, Google Docs or Zoom.
 Q: What is HTTP? Answer: The protocol browsers and servers use to exchange web pages and data.
Teaching Module: Artificial Intelligence and Data Science
Learning roadmap
 Beginner: Python, NumPy and pandas, basic statistics, reading and cleaning data.
 Intermediate: Probability, linear algebra basics, machine learning: regression, classification, clustering.
 Advanced: Deep learning, natural language processing, computer vision, model deployment (MLOps).
Concepts to teach (in order)
1. Dataset, features and labels: A dataset is a collection of examples. Features are the inputs (for
example house size). The label is the answer we want to predict (for example price).
2. Supervised and unsupervised learning: Supervised learning learns from labelled examples, such
as predicting prices. Unsupervised learning finds patterns in unlabelled data, such as grouping similar
customers.
3. Linear regression: It fits a straight line y = mx + c through data so we can predict a number. The
line is chosen to make the total error as small as possible.
4. Overfitting: When a model memorises the training data, including noise, and performs badly on new
data. We reduce it with more data, simpler models and validation.
5. Neural network: A network of connected layers of simple units that learns patterns by adjusting
weights. Deep learning uses many layers.
Mini project: Predict house prices from a dataset, then build a spam message classifier.
Practice questions
 Q: What is overfitting? Answer: The model learns the training data too closely and fails on new data.
 Q: Why do we split data into training and testing sets? Answer: To check how well the model works on
data it has not seen before.
 Q: Is predicting exam marks regression or classification? Answer: Regression, because the output is a
number.
Teaching Module: Cyber Security
Learning roadmap
 Beginner: Networking basics, Linux basics, the CIA triad, common threats such as phishing.
 Intermediate: Cryptography, web application security, firewalls, vulnerability scanning on authorised
labs.
 Advanced: Digital forensics, malware analysis, incident response, security auditing.
Concepts to teach (in order)
1. CIA triad: Confidentiality means only authorised people see data. Integrity means data is not
changed illegally. Availability means systems are working when needed.

Engineering Student Guidance Assistant - Knowledge Base - Page 11
2. Encryption and hashing: Encryption turns data into unreadable form and can be reversed with a
key. Hashing is one-way and is used to store passwords safely.
3. Phishing and social engineering: Attackers trick people, not machines, for example with fake
emails. Defence: check the sender, never share OTPs, do not click unknown links.
4. Injection attacks and defence: Unsafe input can make a database run harmful commands. The
defence is to validate input and use parameterised queries.
5. Firewall and two-factor authentication: A firewall filters network traffic by rules. Two-factor
authentication needs a second proof, such as an OTP, besides the password.
Mini project: Build a password strength checker, and practise legally in a home lab or authorised training
platform only.
Practice questions
 Q: What does CIA stand for in security? Answer: Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability.
 Q: How is hashing different from encryption? Answer: Hashing is one-way; encryption can be reversed
with a key.
 Q: Is ethical hacking legal? Answer: Yes, only with written permission from the system owner.
Teaching Module: Electronics and Communication Engineering
Learning roadmap
 Beginner: Voltage, current, resistance, Ohm's law, resistors, capacitors, diodes.
 Intermediate: Transistors, op-amps, digital logic, microcontrollers such as Arduino.
 Advanced: Signals and systems, communication systems, VLSI, antennas, embedded design.
Concepts to teach (in order)
1. Ohm's law: V = I x R. Voltage equals current times resistance. If V = 10 V and R = 5 ohm, then I = 2
A.
2. Diode: A component that allows current in only one direction. It is used in rectifiers to change AC to
DC.
3. Transistor: A tiny electronic switch or amplifier. It is the building block of all modern chips.
4. Logic gates: AND, OR and NOT gates work on 0 and 1. AND gives 1 only if both inputs are 1.
Combined gates build calculators and computers.
5. Modulation: Adding information to a carrier wave so it can travel far. AM changes the amplitude, FM
changes the frequency.
Mini project: Blink an LED with an Arduino, then build a temperature display with a sensor.
Practice questions
 Q: If V = 12 V and R = 4 ohm, what is the current? Answer: I = V / R = 3 A.
 Q: What is the difference between analog and digital signals? Answer: Analog signals vary
continuously; digital signals have only discrete values such as 0 and 1.
 Q: What is modulation? Answer: Combining the message signal with a carrier wave for transmission.
Teaching Module: Electrical and Electronics Engineering
Learning roadmap
 Beginner: Voltage, current, power, AC and DC, basic circuits and safety.
 Intermediate: Kirchhoff's laws, transformers, DC and AC machines, three-phase supply.
 Advanced: Power systems, power electronics, control systems, renewable energy and electric
vehicles.

Engineering Student Guidance Assistant - Knowledge Base - Page 12
Concepts to teach (in order)
1. Electric power: P = V x I. A 100 W bulb on 230 V draws about 0.43 A.
2. Kirchhoff's laws: KCL: current entering a junction equals current leaving. KVL: the voltages around
a closed loop add up to zero.
3. Transformer: Works on electromagnetic induction and steps AC voltage up or down. It does not
work on DC.
4. Why power is transmitted at high voltage: For the same power, higher voltage means lower
current, and losses (I squared R) are smaller.
5. Motor and generator: A motor converts electrical energy to mechanical energy. A generator does
the opposite.
Mini project: Build a small solar-powered phone charger, or simulate a simple inverter.
Practice questions
 Q: What is the formula for power? Answer: P = V x I.
 Q: Why does a transformer not work on DC? Answer: It needs a changing magnetic field, which only
AC produces.
 Q: What is the main use of a generator? Answer: To convert mechanical energy into electrical energy.
Teaching Module: Mechanical Engineering
Learning roadmap
 Beginner: Forces, units, Newton's laws, stress and strain, engineering drawing.
 Intermediate: Thermodynamics, fluid mechanics, strength of materials, CAD modelling.
 Advanced: Machine design, heat transfer, manufacturing, finite element analysis.
Concepts to teach (in order)
1. Newton's laws: 1: an object keeps its state unless a force acts. 2: F = m x a. 3: every action has an
equal and opposite reaction.
2. Stress and strain: Stress = force / area. Strain = change in length / original length. A 1000 N load on
100 square mm gives 10 N per square mm.
3. First law of thermodynamics: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted from one
form to another.
4. Heat engine and efficiency: A heat engine converts heat into work. Efficiency = useful work output /
heat input. It is never 100 percent.
5. Manufacturing processes: Casting pours molten metal into a mould. Forging shapes metal with
force. Machining cuts material away. 3D printing adds material layer by layer.
Mini project: Design a gear or bracket in CAD software and make a small working model.
Practice questions
 Q: What is torque? Answer: Force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the axis.
 Q: Name the three modes of heat transfer. Answer: Conduction, convection and radiation.
 Q: What is the unit of stress? Answer: Pascal, or newton per square metre.
Teaching Module: Civil Engineering
Learning roadmap
 Beginner: Engineering drawing, building materials (cement, sand, steel, bricks), basic surveying.
 Intermediate: Strength of materials, concrete technology, fluid mechanics, soil mechanics.

Engineering Student Guidance Assistant - Knowledge Base - Page 13
 Advanced: Structural analysis and design, foundation engineering, transportation, estimation and
costing.
Concepts to teach (in order)
1. Concrete and RCC: Concrete is cement, sand, aggregate and water. It is strong in compression but
weak in tension, so steel bars are added to make reinforced cement concrete (RCC).
2. Types of loads: Dead load is the permanent weight of the structure. Live load is people and
furniture. Wind and earthquake loads are also considered.
3. Surveying: Measuring land distances, angles and levels to prepare maps and set out buildings.
Tools: chain, theodolite, total station.
4. Foundation: The part that transfers building load safely to the soil. The type depends on soil
strength.
5. Water-cement ratio: The ratio of water to cement in concrete. A lower ratio gives stronger concrete
if the mix is still workable.
Mini project: Draw a small house plan in AutoCAD and estimate the quantity of cement, sand and bricks.
Practice questions
 Q: Why is steel used in concrete? Answer: Steel handles tension, which concrete is weak at.
 Q: What is a dead load? Answer: The permanent weight of the structure itself.
 Q: What is the purpose of a foundation? Answer: To transfer the structure's load safely to the ground.
Teaching Module: Chemical Engineering
Learning roadmap
 Beginner: Basic chemistry, mole concept, units and conversions, introduction to industrial processes.
 Intermediate: Material and energy balances, fluid mechanics, thermodynamics, heat transfer.
 Advanced: Reaction engineering, mass transfer, process control, plant design and safety.
Concepts to teach (in order)
1. Material balance: Input - output + generation = accumulation. In a steady process with no reaction,
what goes in must come out.
2. Unit operations: Basic steps used in plants, such as distillation, filtration, absorption and
evaporation.
3. Catalyst: A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up.
4. Heat exchanger: Equipment that transfers heat from a hot fluid to a cold fluid without mixing them.
5. Process flow diagram: A drawing that shows equipment and material flow in a plant. Safety studies
such as HAZOP check what could go wrong.
Mini project: Draw a process flow diagram for water purification or ethanol distillation.
Practice questions
 Q: What does a catalyst do? Answer: It speeds up a reaction and is not consumed.
 Q: On what principle does distillation work? Answer: Separation based on differences in boiling points.
 Q: What does a material balance state? Answer: Mass is conserved: input - output + generation =
accumulation.
Teaching Module: Aerospace and Aeronautical Engineering
Learning roadmap
 Beginner: Four forces of flight, parts of an aircraft, basic physics and mathematics.
 Intermediate: Aerodynamics, aircraft structures, propulsion, materials.

Engineering Student Guidance Assistant - Knowledge Base - Page 14
 Advanced: Flight mechanics, orbital mechanics, avionics, computational fluid dynamics.
Concepts to teach (in order)
1. Four forces of flight: Lift, weight, thrust and drag. For steady level flight, lift equals weight and
thrust equals drag.
2. Lift and Bernoulli: A wing is shaped and tilted so air flows faster over the top, giving lower pressure
above and higher pressure below, which creates lift.
3. Angle of attack and stall: If the wing is tilted beyond a critical angle, airflow separates and lift drops
suddenly. This is a stall.
4. Jet engine: Four stages: intake, compression, combustion and exhaust. The exhaust pushes the
aircraft forward.
5. Rocket thrust: Rockets push hot gas backward and get pushed forward (Newton's third law). They
work in space because they carry their own oxidiser.
Mini project: Build a foam glider and test how wing shape affects flight distance, or simulate a model
rocket.
Practice questions
 Q: What is a stall? Answer: Loss of lift when the angle of attack exceeds the critical angle.
 Q: Name the four forces of flight. Answer: Lift, weight, thrust and drag.
 Q: Why can rockets work in space? Answer: They carry fuel and oxidiser and do not need air.
Teaching Module: Automobile Engineering
Learning roadmap
 Beginner: Main parts of a vehicle, the four-stroke engine cycle, basic mechanics.
 Intermediate: Transmission, clutch, brakes, steering, suspension, vehicle electrical systems.
 Advanced: Electric vehicle powertrain, battery management, vehicle dynamics, driver assistance
systems.
Concepts to teach (in order)
1. Four-stroke cycle: Intake, compression, power and exhaust. The crankshaft turns twice per cycle.
2. Clutch and gearbox: The clutch connects or disconnects engine and gearbox. The gearbox
changes torque and speed for different driving conditions.
3. Brakes: Disc brakes squeeze pads on a rotating disc; drum brakes press shoes inside a drum. Both
convert motion into heat.
4. Electric vehicle: Main parts: battery pack, inverter, electric motor and a battery management
system.
5. Regenerative braking: In EVs the motor works as a generator while slowing down, sending energy
back into the battery.
Mini project: Study and make a model of a four-stroke engine, or compare petrol and electric vehicles for
cost and efficiency.
Practice questions
 Q: What are the four strokes? Answer: Intake, compression, power and exhaust.
 Q: What is regenerative braking? Answer: Recovering energy during braking and storing it in the
battery.
 Q: What is the role of the clutch? Answer: To connect or disconnect the engine from the gearbox.
Teaching Module: Mechatronics and Robotics Engineering

Engineering Student Guidance Assistant - Knowledge Base - Page 15
Learning roadmap
 Beginner: Basic electronics, basic mechanics, Arduino programming.
 Intermediate: Sensors and actuators, motors, feedback control, PLC basics.
 Advanced: Robot kinematics, machine vision, ROS, advanced automation.
Concepts to teach (in order)
1. Sensor, controller, actuator: A sensor measures, the controller decides, and the actuator acts. A
line-following robot uses this loop.
2. Feedback control and PID: The controller compares the target with the actual value. P reacts to the
present error, I to past error, D to how fast the error changes.
3. Types of motors: DC motors spin continuously. Servo motors move to a precise angle. Stepper
motors move in exact steps.
4. PLC: A rugged industrial computer used to automate machines and production lines.
5. Degrees of freedom: The number of independent movements a robot arm can make. A typical arm
has 6.
Mini project: Build a line-following robot, then a small robotic arm with servo motors.
Practice questions
 Q: What is the difference between a servo and a stepper motor? Answer: A servo goes to a set angle
using feedback; a stepper moves in fixed steps.
 Q: What is feedback control? Answer: Using measured output to correct the system toward the target.
 Q: Give an example of a sensor. Answer: Ultrasonic distance sensor, temperature sensor or IR
sensor.
Teaching Module: Biomedical Engineering
Learning roadmap
 Beginner: Basic human anatomy and physiology, basic electronics, how medical devices help doctors.
 Intermediate: Biosignals such as ECG and EEG, instrumentation, sensors, signal processing.
 Advanced: Medical imaging, biomaterials, rehabilitation engineering, medical device safety rules.
Concepts to teach (in order)
1. ECG: An electrocardiogram records the heart's electrical activity using electrodes on the skin.
2. Biosensor: A device that detects a biological signal or substance, such as a glucose meter.
3. Medical imaging: X-ray and CT use ionising radiation. Ultrasound uses sound waves. MRI uses
strong magnets and radio waves.
4. Biocompatibility: A material is biocompatible if the body accepts it without harmful reactions.
Needed for implants and prosthetics.
5. Amplification and filtering: Body signals are very weak and noisy, so devices amplify them and
filter out noise.
Mini project: Build a heart-rate monitor with a pulse sensor and Arduino.
Practice questions
 Q: Which imaging methods avoid ionising radiation? Answer: Ultrasound and MRI.
 Q: What does biocompatible mean? Answer: Safe for the body and not causing harmful reactions.
 Q: Why do ECG devices need amplifiers? Answer: Heart signals are very small.
Teaching Module: Biotechnology Engineering
Learning roadmap

Engineering Student Guidance Assistant - Knowledge Base - Page 16
 Beginner: Cell structure, basic biochemistry, basic chemistry and biology of microbes.
 Intermediate: Genetics, molecular biology, microbiology, enzymes.
 Advanced: Bioprocess engineering, genetic engineering, bioinformatics, downstream processing.
Concepts to teach (in order)
1. Central dogma: DNA is copied to RNA, and RNA is used to make proteins.
2. Enzymes: Proteins that speed up biological reactions. Used in medicines, detergents and food.
3. PCR: Polymerase chain reaction makes millions of copies of a DNA piece. Used in diagnostics and
research.
4. Fermentation and bioreactor: Microbes grown in controlled tanks to make products such as
antibiotics, vaccines and ethanol.
5. Bioinformatics: Using computers to study biological data, such as comparing DNA sequences.
Mini project: Extract DNA from fruit in a safe lab, and compare gene sequences with free online tools.
Practice questions
 Q: What is the central dogma? Answer: DNA to RNA to protein.
 Q: What is PCR used for? Answer: To copy and amplify a specific piece of DNA.
 Q: What is the role of enzymes? Answer: They speed up biochemical reactions.
Teaching Module: Industrial and Production Engineering
Learning roadmap
 Beginner: Manufacturing basics, basic statistics, engineering drawing.
 Intermediate: Work study, quality control, operations research, production planning.
 Advanced: Supply chain, lean and six sigma, simulation, ergonomics.
Concepts to teach (in order)
1. Lean: A way of working that removes waste such as waiting, extra movement, defects and
overproduction.
2. Six Sigma: A method to reduce defects and variation using data. The steps are Define, Measure,
Analyse, Improve, Control.
3. Economic Order Quantity: The order size that gives the lowest total of ordering cost and holding
cost.
4. Linear programming: A mathematical method to get the best result, such as maximum profit, under
limits like material and time.
5. Control chart: A graph that shows whether a process is stable or going out of control over time.
Mini project: Study the process of a small workshop, draw the flow and suggest improvements.
Practice questions
 Q: What does lean aim to remove? Answer: Waste.
 Q: What is a control chart used for? Answer: Monitoring whether a process stays stable.
 Q: What is EOQ? Answer: The order quantity that minimises total ordering and holding cost.
Teaching Module: Environmental Engineering
Learning roadmap
 Beginner: Ecosystems, types of pollution, basic chemistry and biology.
 Intermediate: Water chemistry, air pollution, solid waste management, environmental laws.
 Advanced: Treatment plant design, environmental impact assessment, climate and sustainability.

Engineering Student Guidance Assistant - Knowledge Base - Page 17
Concepts to teach (in order)
1. Water treatment steps: Screening, coagulation, sedimentation, filtration and disinfection.
2. BOD and COD: BOD is the oxygen microbes need to break down organic matter in water. COD is
the oxygen needed to chemically oxidise all pollutants. Higher values mean more pollution.
3. Air pollutants: Examples: PM2.5, nitrogen oxides, sulphur dioxide and carbon monoxide. PM2.5 is
tiny and can enter the lungs and blood.
4. Waste hierarchy: Reduce first, then reuse, then recycle, then recover energy, and dispose of waste
last.
5. Environmental Impact Assessment: A study done before a project to find its effects on air, water,
soil and people, and ways to reduce harm.
Mini project: Test local water samples for pH and TDS, or design a rainwater harvesting system for a
building.
Practice questions
 Q: What does high BOD show? Answer: Heavy organic pollution in the water.
 Q: Why is PM2.5 dangerous? Answer: The particles are small enough to reach deep into the lungs
and blood.
 Q: What comes first in the waste hierarchy? Answer: Reduce.
Part 6: Frequently Asked Questions
Question: Which engineering branch is the best?
Answer: No branch is best for everyone. The best branch is the one that matches the student's interest,
strengths and career goal. The assistant compares options instead of declaring a single winner.
Question: I am confused between CSE and IT. What is the difference?
Answer: Both involve software and programming. CSE is broader and includes theory, algorithms and
systems. IT focuses more on applications, networks and managing information systems. Job options are
very similar.
Question: I am weak in mathematics. Can I still do engineering?
Answer: Yes, but mathematics is important in most branches, especially AI and Data Science, ECE and
EEE. The student can improve with regular practice, and branches such as IT, Civil or Industrial
Engineering can be good starting points.
Question: Which branches are good for coding?
Answer: Computer Science and Engineering, Information Technology, Artificial Intelligence and Data
Science, and Cyber Security. Electronics and Mechatronics also use programming.
Question: Which branches are good for hardware and machines?
Answer: Mechanical, Electrical, Electronics and Communication, Automobile, Mechatronics and
Aerospace Engineering.
Question: Which branch suits a student who likes biology?
Answer: Biotechnology Engineering and Biomedical Engineering.
Question: Can I change my branch after admission?
Answer: Branch change rules depend on the institute and university, and usually depend on marks and
seat availability. The assistant advises contacting the admission office.

Engineering Student Guidance Assistant - Knowledge Base - Page 18
Question: Can the assistant teach me my chosen domain?
Answer: Yes. After the introduction, the assistant asks the student's domain and level, shows a roadmap,
and teaches concept by concept with examples, check questions and practice questions (Part 5).
Question: Will I get a job after engineering?
Answer: Job opportunities depend on skills, projects, internships and marks as well as the branch. The
assistant cannot guarantee jobs or salary.
Question: What should I do if I use bad words by mistake?
Answer: The assistant gives a polite reminder. The student can continue by using respectful language.

title: AI Engineering Tutor — Conversation Design
content:
AI Engineering Tutor — Conversation Design
Flow: greeting → name & age → student's doubt → teaching, with example conversations for both a
smooth (positive) session and a difficult (negative) one.
Conversation Flow
1. Greeting — Casual hello, nothing technical yet.
2. Name and age — Asked naturally, in two short questions, not like a form.
3. Doubt — Ask what the student is stuck on or curious about.
4. Teach — Adapt explanation depth to the stated age, teach in short steps.
Example 1 — Positive Conversation
The student answers clearly and stays engaged. The tutor moves forward one step at a time.
Tutor: Hey! Welcome in. Before we start, what should I call you?
Student: Riya
Tutor: Nice to meet you, Riya. How old are you, just so I can pitch explanations at the right level?
Student: 16
Tutor: Got it. So what's on your mind today — something you're stuck on, or just curious about?
Student: I don't get how recursion works in code
Tutor: Good one to ask about. Think of recursion like Russian nesting dolls: each doll holds a smaller
one, until you reach the tiniest doll that doesn't open anymore. In code, a function calls itself on a smaller
problem until it hits a “base case” that stops it. Want to see a tiny example, like counting down from 5?
Student: yes
Tutor: [shows a short countdown function, then asks Riya to predict the output]
Example 2 — Negative Conversation (resistance, frustration, wrong
answer)
The tutor does not force the name/age questions, acknowledges frustration, narrows a vague complaint to one
concrete thing, and walks the student to the fix instead of just giving the answer.
Tutor: Hey! Before we dive in, what's your name?
Student: why do you need that
Tutor: No pressure, you can skip it. I just use it to keep the chat personal. What should I call you?
Student: fine, Arjun

title: AI Engineering Tutor — Conversation Design
content:
Tutor: Thanks, Arjun. And how old are you, roughly? Helps me pick the right level of explanation.
Student: does it matter just teach me
Tutor: Fair enough, we can skip that too. What are you stuck on?
Student: everything, I hate this subject
Tutor: That's frustrating, and it's okay to feel that way. Let's pick just one small thing instead of everything.
What were you working on right before you got stuck?
Student: some loop thing, it keeps giving wrong numbers
Tutor: Let's look at it together. Can you paste the loop, or tell me what numbers you expected versus
what you got?
Student: [pastes code with an off-by-one error]
Tutor: I see it. Your loop starts at 1 but the array starts at 0, so it's skipping the first item. Try changing the
start to 0 and run it again — what do you get?
Student: oh it works now
Tutor: Nice catch. Want to try one more loop to lock that in, or move to something else?
Design Rules for the Prompt
- Ask for name and age only once, lightly. If the student resists or skips, do not insist
— move on.
- If the student shows frustration or gives a vague answer (“everything”), narrow the
question to one small thing instead of pushing them to pick a whole topic.
- If the student gives a wrong answer, do not just correct it. Point at what's likely
wrong and ask them to try again before giving the fix.
- Match explanation depth to stated age when given; default to a general teen/adult level
if age is skipped.
- Never make the student feel bad for not knowing something.
